posts.title: Why Most Kenyan Brand Refreshes Fail (and What to Do Instead)
posts.excerpt: A rebrand is not a logo change. It's a strategic repositioning. Here's how to know the difference before you spend the budget.
posts.body:
Most brand refreshes in Kenya are sold as a logo, a new colour, and a launch party. Eighteen months later the business looks the same and the market behaves the same. The reason is simple: a refresh that only touches the surface cannot change how a brand is understood.

## A rebrand is a repositioning, not a repaint

When a business changes its logo but keeps the same promise, the same audience, and the same message, customers experience it as noise. A true repositioning starts with a decision about who the brand is for and what it stands for — then every visible choice flows from that.

## The test before you spend

Before signing a refresh, answer three questions: (1) What belief about our customer changed? (2) What will the market now understand that it didn't before? (3) What will we stop doing? If you can't answer these, you're repainting, not repositioning.

## What to do instead

Start with research, not design. Map where you are understood and where you're not. Pick one sharp position. Then let identity, tone, and campaign all serve that single idea. The visual change is the last 10%, not the project.

posts.meta_description: A rebrand is not a logo change. Learn the difference between a surface refresh and a real repositioning before you spend the budget.

posts.title: The TikTok Playbook for African Brands: What Works, What Doesn't
posts.excerpt: We've run 23 TikTok campaigns for African brands. The results are counterintuitive. Here's what we've learned.
posts.body:
After running 23 TikTok campaigns for African brands, the pattern is clear: the brands that win treat the platform like a culture, not a billboard.

## What doesn't work

Polished TVCs cut into vertical format. Corporate voice. A hard sell in the first three seconds. TikTok's algorithm rewards watch-time, and watch-time comes from people feeling something — usually amusement, recognition, or belonging.

## What does work

Native creators, not celebrity ads. A single relatable insight about being African, Kenyan, or part of a specific scene. Sound that's made for the platform, not licensed from a library. And a willingness to let the brand be the side character, not the hero.

## The counterintuitive part

The best-performing videos often have the weakest logo presence. The brand wins by being woven into a moment people wanted to watch anyway.

posts.title: Understanding Gen Z in Nairobi: The Consumer Brands Need to Win
posts.excerpt: Primary research with 400 Nairobi Gen Z consumers. Their relationship with brands is fundamentally different.
posts.body:
We spoke with 400 Nairobi Gen Z consumers. The headline: this generation does not separate 'brand' from 'behaviour.' They expect the companies they buy from to act like people they'd actually respect.

## Trust is earned in public

Gen Z in Nairobi watches how a brand treats its staff, responds to criticism, and shows up during a crisis. A flawless ad with a tone-deaf reply thread undoes the whole thing.

## Identity over aspiration

Older marketing sold who you could become. This group buys who you already are. Brands that reflect real Nairobi life — language, humour, struggle — outperform aspirational fantasy.

## What brands should do

Be consistent across touchpoints, respond like a human, and don't pretend to be something you're not. Authenticity isn't a tone; it's alignment between what you say and what you do.

posts.title: Colour in African Brand Identity: Moving Beyond Pan-African Cliché
posts.excerpt: How African brands can draw on local visual culture without falling into the trap of decorative tokenism.
posts.body:
Green, gold, red, and black are everywhere on the continent — and increasingly they mean nothing. When every brand reaches for the same palette, distinctiveness dies.

## The cliché problem

Pan-African colours signal 'African' instantly, but they also signal 'same as everyone else.' A brand built only on cliché is forgettable the moment it leaves the screen.

## Drawing from culture, not costume

Real visual distinctiveness comes from specifics: a pattern from a particular community, a colour found in a local landscape, a type treatment rooted in a script or signage tradition. The more specific, the more ownable.

## The standard

Use heritage as a source, not a costume. The work must illuminate something true about the brand, not just reference the continent.

posts.title: The One-Sentence Positioning Test: Is Your Brand Actually Clear?
posts.excerpt: If you can't explain what your brand is and who it's for in one sentence, you don't have a positioning. You have a description.
posts.body:
Here is the test we give every new client. Fill in the blank out loud:

'For [who], [brand] is the [category] that [single sharp difference].'

If you can't, you don't have a positioning yet. You have a description.

## Why one sentence matters

A positioning that takes a paragraph to explain will take a paragraph to forget. The brands that own a category can be stated in a single breath — and so can the brief that builds everything else.

## What to do with it

Write the sentence. Put it where everyone can see it. Measure every campaign, page, and product decision against it. If something doesn't serve the sentence, it doesn't ship.

posts.title: The State of African Fintech Branding: A 2025 Review
posts.excerpt: How Kenya's fintech brands are positioning and communicating — and what the category leaders are doing differently.
posts.body:
2025 was the year African fintech stopped looking like banks and started looking like lifestyle apps. We reviewed the category's leading Kenyan brands to see what actually separates the memorable from the me-too.

## The trust paradox

Fintech sells money, the most trust-sensitive product there is, yet the category leaned into playful, consumer-app aesthetics. The leaders resolved the paradox with relentless clarity about what they do and proof, not promises.

## What leaders do differently

They name a specific job ('send money home, free') instead of a vague mission ('financial inclusion for all'). They use motion and microcopy to feel human. And they keep the brand tight across product, support, and marketing.

## The outlook

As the category matures, distinctiveness — not feature lists — will decide who survives the next consolidation.

posts.title: The Quiet Power of African Minimalism
posts.excerpt: Minimalism in African brand design isn't emptiness — it's confidence. Here's how restraint reads as premium.
posts.body:
Minimalism is often mistaken for absence. On African brands, restraint reads differently: it signals confidence, not lack.

## Restraint as a statement

When a brand removes the decorative clutter, what remains must carry weight. The logo, the colour, the type — each becomes a decision, not a default.

> A minimal brand is not one with less; it is one with nothing unnecessary.

## Avoiding the cold minimal trap

Western minimalism can feel cold. African minimalism should feel intentional — warm negative space, a single resonant colour, a typeface with character.

## The payoff

Premium perception follows clarity. When customers understand you instantly, they trust you faster.

> On WhatsApp, the brand that listens wins the relationship.

## Guardrails

Never spam. Permission and pace matter more than volume.

posts.title: Brand Architecture for the African Conglomerate
posts.excerpt: As African companies diversify, the house-of-brands vs branded-house decision decides whether scale helps or dilutes.
posts.body:
Diversification is the African growth story. But every new division forces a question: one masterbrand, or a portfolio?

## Two models

Branded house (Safaricom) builds one equity. House of brands (many FMCG groups) lets each product stand alone.

## The cost of muddy architecture

When everything shares a name but not a promise, customers get confused and the masterbrand erodes.

> Architecture is strategy made visible.

## A simple test

If a new product would damage the parent's meaning, it needs its own name.

Aspirational-but-accessible pricing built entire categories in Africa. It's a brand stance, not a discount.

## Anchoring with tiers

A premium tier makes the core offer feel considered, not cheap.

> Price is the brand's first sentence.

## Avoid the race to zero

Competing only on price erases the brand. Compete on meaning.

Customers remember what they see often, said the same way.

## Systems over heroics

A reliable template outperforms a one-off masterpiece.

> Consistency is brilliance repeated.

## Audit the drift

Brands drift silently; check quarterly.

posts.title: Inside a Zareya Rebrand: The Six Weeks the Case Study Never Shows
posts.excerpt: The real week-by-week anatomy of a rebrand at Zareya — the field work, the fights, and the boardroom moment that nearly kills every project.
posts.body:
Every rebrand looks inevitable in the case study. The deck shows the old logo, then the new one, and the space between them reads like destiny. What the deck never shows is the six weeks in the middle — the arguments, the dead ends, the moment the client's CEO nearly killed the whole direction over a shade of green.

This is what that middle actually looks like inside Zareya. Not the sanitised version. The real sequence, week by week, including the parts that go wrong on schedule.

## Week one: the interrogation

We don't open Figma in week one. We open a meeting room and we ask uncomfortable questions. Who buys you when they could buy the cheaper option — and why? What did your last three customers say when they complained? If your brand vanished tomorrow, who in Nairobi would genuinely notice?

The founders usually answer the first two confidently and go quiet on the third. That silence is the brief. A rebrand that starts from "we want to look more modern" fails. A rebrand that starts from "nobody would notice if we disappeared" has something real to fix.

We also pull the receipts: sales data, churn reasons, customer-service transcripts, the WhatsApp messages the sales team actually sends. Brands live in those messages far more than they live in the brand guidelines PDF nobody has opened since 2022.

## Week two: the field

Strategy written in an office in Kilimani describes Kilimani. So we leave. We sit in the client's shops, ride the routes their distributors ride, and watch real customers pick the product up, turn it over, and put it back. Ten minutes of watching someone hesitate at a shelf teaches you more about your packaging than a month of internal debate.

This is also where we test the competitive set honestly. Not the competitors the client names — the ones the customer names. They are rarely the same list. A Nairobi fintech thinks it competes with other fintechs. Its customers think it competes with the mattress, the chama, and M-PESA's paybill.

> The customer's shortlist is the only shortlist. Everything else is corporate vanity.

## Weeks three and four: the fight

Now the studio work starts, and with it the productive conflict. We build two or three strategic territories — not moodboards, territories. Each one is a full argument: this is who we are for, this is the enemy, this is what we say and refuse to say, and this is roughly how it looks and sounds.

Then we try to kill them. Internally first. If a territory can be claimed word-for-word by the client's biggest competitor, it dies. If it only works with a big media budget behind it, it dies. If it needs a paragraph to explain, it dies. What survives is usually the option that felt slightly too sharp in the first review — the one someone in the room called "risky."

This is the week clients get nervous, and they should. Distinctive positions feel exposed before they feel right. Safe positions feel right immediately and then do nothing for five years.

## Week five: the green moment

Every project has one. Ours have included a CEO who hated a colour because it belonged to his former employer, a board member who wanted the logo bigger on everything, and a founder who loved a direction until his cousin didn't. This is not a design problem. It is a decision-rights problem, and we solve it in week one by agreeing — in writing — who has the final call and what evidence can overrule taste.

When the green moment comes, we go back to that agreement and back to the field work. Taste argues with taste forever. Taste loses to a photograph of real customers choosing the shelf. Evidence is how the work survives the boardroom.

## Week six: the unglamorous part

The reveal is five percent of the job. The other ninety-five percent is making the brand survivable: templates the intern can use without breaking anything, a voice guide with real examples of WhatsApp replies and job ads — not adjectives — and a rollout sequence that starts with the touchpoints customers actually meet. In most Kenyan businesses that means the M-PESA till confirmation, the delivery rider, and the signage, long before the website.

We also leave a kill list: the old assets that must disappear, with owners and dates. Rebrands don't fail at launch. They fail three months later, when the old letterhead resurfaces because nobody deleted it.

## What the case study hides

The finished work looks inevitable because everything that didn't survive is invisible. But the value was in the fights — the territory that died, the colour that got overruled by evidence, the week we spent watching people not buy the product.

If your agency's process has no visible arguments in it, you're not buying strategy. You're buying decoration with a timeline.

posts.title: The Nairobi Creative Economy: Who Actually Pays for the Work
posts.excerpt: Nairobi's creative sector is loud on output, quiet on economics. Who actually funds the work, why the mid-market is missing, and what agencies can change.
posts.body:
Nairobi does not have a creativity problem. Walk through Kilimani on any given Tuesday and you will pass three studios producing work that would hold its own in Lagos, Cape Town or London. What Nairobi has is an economics problem — a structural gap between the people who make the work and the money that funds it.

What follows is an agency-side view, not a survey. It describes the shape of the briefs that cross our desk, the budgets attached to them, and the conversations that happen just before a contract is signed or quietly abandoned.

## Four wallets, four logics

Creative money in Nairobi arrives from roughly four sources, and each behaves according to its own rules.

Multinationals and regional FMCG hold the largest budgets and the longest approval chains. The brief usually lands pre-cooked from a regional hub, and the local mandate is adaptation rather than origination. The revenue is dependable. The creative latitude is not.

Banks, telcos and fintech spend heavily and continuously, but procurement owns the relationship. Work is bought through framework agreements and rate cards, reviewed quarterly, and priced per deliverable. This is the closest thing Nairobi has to a stable creative industry, and it is also where good strategy most often gets converted into production line output.

The development sector moves real money and reaches real audiences, but its logic is reporting rather than markets. Deliverables track grant cycles instead of buying cycles, and brand coherence is routinely traded away to satisfy funder visibility requirements. Agencies that live here get very good at compliance and slowly forget how to sell things.

Then there are SMEs and founder-led businesses. The most interesting briefs in the city sit in this group, alongside the thinnest budgets and the fastest decisions. A founder can approve a full identity in one meeting. That same founder often cannot fund the second phase.

## The missing middle

Put those four together and the shape of the market becomes clear. Nairobi has premium work at the top and volume work at the bottom, with very little in between.

The missing tier is the mid-market brand programme: a business with real revenue, no in-house marketing team, and enough ambition to fund a proper positioning exercise rather than a logo. In mature markets this tier carries the industry. Here it barely exists, because the businesses that belong in it have been trained by experience to expect one of two things — a cheap logo from a freelancer or an intimidating quote from an agency built to serve banks.

Neither option fits, so the work does not happen. This is not a demand failure. It is a packaging failure, and it belongs to the agencies.

## Talent trains here, then bills elsewhere

Remote work has repriced Nairobi's best designers, and the repricing was permanent. A senior designer invoicing a European or American client is not comparing your offer to the local market. They are comparing it to what they already earn from a laptop in their own front room.

Agencies that respond by matching salary alone will lose anyway, because salary is the one axis where they cannot win. What they can offer is the thing freelancing cannot: range, mentorship, work at a scale no individual gets access to, and a portfolio that opens doors five years out. Studios that articulate this keep their people. Studios that treat it as a bidding war train talent for someone else.

> The question is no longer whether Nairobi can produce world-class creative work. It is whether Nairobi can build businesses that keep the people who produce it.

## Three shifts that change the maths

Price the thinking, not the file. Strategy is the highest-value thing an agency does and the most commonly given away free during a pitch. If positioning work is bundled into a design quote, the client learns that it costs nothing. Sell it as a discrete engagement with its own scope, its own price and its own deliverable, and it becomes defensible.

Productise the mid-market. The businesses in the missing middle do not need a bespoke proposal each time. They need a fixed-scope, fixed-price, fixed-timeline programme they can say yes to without a procurement process. Standardise it, name it, publish the price. Predictability is what unlocks that tier.

Build assets, not just invoices. Every agency in this city is trading hours for shillings, which caps growth at headcount. Templates, tools, research the market cannot get elsewhere, licensed frameworks, products of your own — these keep earning after the retainer ends. Almost nobody in Nairobi is doing this seriously, which is precisely why it is available.

## The honest conclusion

The Nairobi creative economy is not underfunded so much as badly structured. The money exists. It is concentrated in clients who buy execution, mediated by procurement teams who buy line items, and largely inaccessible to the businesses who would most benefit from strategic work.

Fixing that is not a policy question or a talent question. It is a commercial design question, and it sits squarely with the agencies. The studios that solve it in the next few years will not be the most creative ones in the city. They will be the ones that finally built a business model to match the work.

posts.title: Typeface as Territory: Why African Brands Still Borrow Their Letterforms
posts.excerpt: Most African brands pick their fonts from the same global shortlist. Typography is territory — and borrowed letterforms quietly cost you distinctiveness.
posts.body:
Walk down Kimathi Street and photograph twenty shopfronts, delivery bikes and app icons. Now strip out the colour and cover the names. What is left is a remarkably uniform alphabet: a geometric sans, lightly rounded, generously tracked — Poppins, Montserrat, or whatever the template shipped with. The same alphabet is running a Lagos fintech, a Kigali logistics startup and a Johannesburg property fund.

Brand teams will spend three weeks arguing about a shade of green and forty minutes picking a typeface. That is backwards. Colour is the first thing a customer notices and the easiest thing a competitor copies. Type is what they read for the next four years — every price, every terms page, every push notification at 8pm. It is the highest-mileage design decision most brands make by default.

## The shortlist is a distinctiveness tax

There is nothing wrong with Montserrat. There is something very wrong with eleven companies in the same category using it. Distinctiveness in brand building is not a nice-to-have; it is the mechanism by which memory works. If a customer cannot tell your ad from your competitor's ad at a glance, your media spend is subsidising the category, not your business.

Type carries more of that recognition load than most teams assume. Readers do not consciously register letterforms, but they register texture — the rhythm of a paragraph, the weight of a headline, the shape of a price. Change the typeface and a brand feels different before anyone can say why. Keep the default typeface and you inherit whatever everyone else already feels.

> Colour gets you noticed. Type gets you remembered — or forgotten, one paragraph at a time.

## "African typography" is not a display font

The reflex correction is worse than the problem. A brand realises it looks generic, so it reaches for a novelty display face with faux-carved serifs and calls it heritage. That is costume. It is the typographic equivalent of putting a kikoi on a stock photo.

Real typographic specificity on this continent comes from harder places. It comes from the scripts we actually write in — Ge'ez, Ajami, Tifinagh, N'Ko — and from extended Latin that most Western foundries treat as an afterthought. Ask a foundry whether their font supports Yoruba's dotted vowels and subscript marks, or Igbo's ị and ụ, or full Amharic. Many will not have an answer. If a brand operates across Nairobi, Lagos and Addis, character coverage is not a technicality. It is whether your brand can spell your customers' names.

It also comes from vernacular sources that are genuinely ours and genuinely ignored: matatu lettering, duka signwriting, hand-painted barbershop boards, kanga borders. Not to be traced literally, but to be read for principles — how weight is used for emphasis, how tight the counters run, how happily the hand mixes systems in one line.

## Where the differentiation actually lives

Most African brands cannot fund a bespoke typeface. A commissioned family runs well into five figures in dollars, which is unserious for a company still proving retention. The good news is that a custom font is rarely where the value sits. Four cheaper levers do most of the work.

**Pairing logic.** A distinctive pairing beats a distinctive font. A quiet workhorse sans for interface and body, paired with something with a real point of view for headlines, creates a signature no single font achieves alone.

**One altered glyph.** Modify the logotype, not the whole family. A single cut counter, an extended terminal, a redrawn ampersand — done once, in the wordmark — gives ownership at a fraction of the cost and licensing risk.

**A system, not a palette.** Most brand guidelines list two fonts and stop. The useful version specifies hierarchy: what a price looks like, what an error message looks like, minimum sizes on a 5-inch screen, how numerals behave in a table. Systems survive junior designers and agency changes. Palettes do not.

**Performance.** A three-weight subset that loads on a patchy 3G connection in Kisii will do more for brand experience than a beautiful nine-weight family that blocks render. Subset aggressively, self-host, and test on the phones your customers actually own — not the one on your desk.

## The licensing conversation nobody has

Web font licences are usually priced by monthly pageviews, and most African brands buy the wrong tier or ignore the terms entirely. Then a campaign works, traffic spikes, and the brand is quietly out of compliance on its own homepage. Check the tier. Check whether the licence covers apps, embedded PDFs and out-of-home artwork. Open-source families like the Google Fonts library are legitimate choices — just choose the ones your category has not already exhausted, and put the saved budget into a custom wordmark.

## Three tests before you sign off

**The blur test.** Blur a headline until words are unreadable. Is the texture still yours, or is it anyone's?

**The screenshot test.** Put your app screen beside three competitors', greyscale. Can a stranger sort them?

**The language test.** Set a customer's full name, in the languages you actually serve, in every weight. If anything breaks, tofu-boxes or falls back to a system font, the font is not fit for the market.

None of this requires a bigger budget. It requires treating letterforms as a strategic asset instead of the last checkbox before launch.
